description: Firebot by Jellyfire is a retro-inspired learning platform that guides beginner and intermediate users through NASA's extensive history of microgravity fire experiments, making complex research accessible and engaging.
summary: NASA FireBot is an AI-powered research assistant that turns decades of NASA microgravity-combustion and spacecraft fire-safety literature into one navigable dashboard. It pairs a Flutter web app styled as a retro CRT terminal — with tiled windows, a linked-note knowledge graph, and keyboard support — with a Gemini retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) backend. Users browse a structured 60+ paper curriculum, explore notes in a force-directed graph, review ranked investigations, compare experiments side-by-side, and chat with "FireBot," which answers every question with grounded citations to the source paper, page, and relevant figures. The corpus is chunked and embedded so each query retrieves the most relevant passages rather than relying on a model's memory alone. It addresses the "Flame in Freefall" challenge by summarizing, ranking, and interpreting scattered combustion research — turning dense, PDF-bound data into fast, cited, conversational insights that directly support safer spacecraft and lunar-habitat design.
details:
FireBot: AI-Powered Microgravity Fire Research Assistant

The Challenge

NASA FireBot is an AI-powered research assistant built for NASA Space Apps' "Flame in Freefall" challenge, which asked teams to summarize, rank, and interpret decades of microgravity combustion research into actionable fire-safety insights. The problem is real: NASA's findings on how fire behaves in space are scattered across dozens of dense technical papers, each locked in a PDF. Hard to find, harder to compare, and nearly impossible for a non-specialist to query. FireBot turns that corpus into a single, navigable interface.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

At its core is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. We assembled a corpus of over 60 NASA technical papers spanning 1974 to 2026, split each into page-tagged chunks of roughly 400 words with 50-word overlap, and embedded every chunk with Google's Gemini embedding model into 3,072-dimensional vectors. When a user asks a question, the query is embedded the same way, the most similar chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity, and those passages, together with their paper number, title, and page, are passed to Gemini as context. The model answers only from that context and cites its sources, so responses are grounded in real research rather than the model's memory. The pipeline also links each cited chunk to the figures from nearby pages, so the actual diagrams and experiment photos surface inside the chat.

Research Interface

That intelligence is wrapped in a deliberately retro interface: a monochrome CRT-style terminal rendered in Flutter for the web. The dashboard is a tiled window manager where users can open a command terminal, browse a structured curriculum of 30+ lessons (each in four levels, from overview to quiz), keep linked markdown research notes, and explore a force-directed knowledge graph that maps how those notes connect. A ranked investigations view scores real microgravity experiments by relevance, and a comparison mode places any two side-by-side so users can spot what is consistent, what conflicts, and what remains unknown. FireBot itself lives in a chat tile with adjustable verbosity, so a researcher and a student get different depths from the same answer.

Impact and Benefits

The benefits are immediate. Time-to-answer drops from hours of PDF searching to seconds. Every claim is traceable to a source. The ranking and comparison views surface cross-experiment patterns that would otherwise require tedious manual cross-referencing. And because the app runs in a browser with full touch and keyboard support, it works equally well on a phone, a laptop, or a classroom projector.

The intended impact is safer spaceflight. Understanding how flames ignite, spread, and extinguish in microgravity is foundational to designing fire-safe spacecraft, habitats, and mission protocols for the Moon and Mars. By making that research accessible, citable, and conversational, FireBot lowers the barrier for engineers, mission planners, students, and the public to build on NASA's hard-won knowledge.

Technology Stack

FireBot was built with Flutter and Dart for the frontend and Python and Flask for the backend, powered by Google's Gemini API for both embeddings and chat. Vector math uses NumPy; the CRT look is achieved with custom GLSL fragment shaders (a scanline pass and a Kawase-blur glass pass). The frontend deploys to Vercel and the backend to Render via Docker, with Git and GitHub for collaboration. No special hardware is required; it runs entirely in a web browser.

Creative Direction

The project's creativity lies in its framing. We chose the aesthetic of an old phosphor terminal, Fallout-green with scanlines, a blinking cursor, and a drifting starfield, so that interacting with modern AI feels like exploring a mission console. Eleven switchable themes, adjustable glass transparency, and a cursor-following sonar turn navigation into part of the experience. The knowledge graph renders notes as a constellation users can pull apart, and every tile, list, and menu is reachable by touch or keyboard.

Accuracy and Accessibility

Finally, our team prioritized accuracy, honesty, and accessibility. The system cites every source and explicitly says when an answer isn't in the corpus rather than inventing one. We kept the interface usable on mobile and desktop, tuned performance for real deployments, and preserved provenance end-to-end. Every chunk remembers its paper and page, so every figure and citation can be traced back to the original document.
